payload.name: Expand abstract positive-evaluative queries with concrete vocabulary
payload.description: Use when a question asks what someone recently did that was rewarding, fulfilling, or a main stressor.
content: If the question uses abstract positive descriptors like 'rewarding experience', 'fulfilling', or 'sense of accomplishment' and the initial retrieval does not return an event memory that explicitly describes an achievement or positive outcome, run an additional keyword or structured search using concrete achievement verbs and nouns (e.g., 'presented', 'conference', 'received positive feedback', 'award', 'recognized').

Before answering a question about a person's main stressor, source of stress, or biggest difficulty, issue searches that go beyond the literal question wording: include stress-related synonyms (stressful, tough, difficult, hard, pressure, overwhelmed) and common life domains (work, family, school, health, finances, relationships).

If the question explicitly excludes a topic ('besides X', 'other than X', 'apart from X'), do not let that excluded topic dominate the query; run an additional search replacing the excluded topic with likely alternative domains.
Do not answer from an indirect memory that only implies the stressor through an overlap or trade-off; keep searching until a memory explicitly states what is stressful, tough, or difficult.

payload.name: activity-participation_search_for_hobbies
payload.description: Use when answering questions about what hobbies, interests, or new activities a person considered, tried, or enjoys; run complementary searches with participation phrasing (e.g., 'attends a class', 'enjoys [activity]') and concrete activity terms before answering.
content: When the question asks about hobbies, interests, or activities a person considered/tried/enjoys, do not answer after a single search phrased with meta-labels like 'considered trying'. Run at least one additional search using participation frames: '[subject] attends/is taking/learns [activity]', '[subject] enjoys [activity]', '[subject] is practicing [activity]'.

For each candidate activity surfaced in any retrieved memory (including classes, sports, or pastimes), search for that concrete activity name, and include preference/event/plan memory kinds covering interests, recreation, and intents.

Before finalizing the answer, verify that the evidence covers all activities the user asks about; if retrieved results contain only general descriptions without concrete activity names, issue broader complementary searches rather than answering from partial evidence.

payload.name: Broaden kind and time filters for ongoing activity queries
payload.description: When a question asks what someone read, used, owned, or was engaged in during a time period, search across event, preference, and state memories without strict point-time filtering, because ongoing activities are often recorded as preferences or states.
content: When a query asks about an activity (reading, using, working on, owning) within a time period, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; include 'preference' and 'state' memories that describe ongoing activities or current status.

Avoid point time_mode filters that exclude records whose world_start is near but after the target period; instead search without a strict time window first, then evaluate temporal relevance from the evidence.

For questions that name a time period (e.g., mid-August 2023, early June, during 2023), use a time_range spanning the full period instead of a single point-in-time target, so events whose start date falls later in the period are still retrieved.

payload.name: Retrieve activities for experience-based advice
payload.description: When a question asks what advice or lessons a person would give based on their experiences or personal growth, also search for their hobbies, interests, and stress-relieving activities, not only explicit advice memories.
content: When the question asks what advice, lessons, or recommendations someone would give based on their experiences or personal growth, do not rely only on explicit advice/support memories. Run additional searches for the person's hobbies, interests, and stress-relieving activities, prioritizing 'preference' and 'event' memories about pastimes such as outdoor, creative, or travel activities.

Before answering, verify whether the retrieved evidence includes such activity memories; if not, issue a new varied search with activity-oriented keywords and treat the found activities as evidence for the advice.

payload.name: Broaden retrieval for alternative path questions
payload.description: When a question asks what alternative career or path someone might consider after a known role or domain, also search for the person's broader interests, values, and activities outside that domain.
content: If the question asks what alternative career or path someone might consider after a named activity/domain, do not limit retrieval to that domain. Run at least one additional search using the person's other hobbies, interests, knowledge, routines, and activities (e.g., pet care, volunteering, creative work) as query terms.

Before answering, check whether any retrieved evidence outside the named domain shows relevant skill or enjoyment; if present, ground the answer in that evidence rather than only in memories from the named domain.

payload.name: Attribute-Synonym Search Expansion
payload.description: Use when a question asks for a specific attribute value (breed, type, color, age) and initial searches return only generic entity mentions.
content: When a user asks for a specific attribute (breed, type, color, age, etc.) of an entity and retrieved memories mention the entity but none explicitly state the attribute, run additional searches using synonym families of the attribute and common value descriptors (e.g., mix, mutt, cross for breed; approximate age phrases for age) instead of repeating the question's exact wording.

After each expanded search, inspect the full text of candidate memories, including their subject and object fields, for any explicit attribute statement; use only evidence from retrieved/current versions when answering, and if the value is still absent, say it is not found rather than guessing.

payload.name: Avoid anchoring on first topic when retrieving specific events
payload.description: Use when a question about a specific past event (what someone shared/made/photographed/posted in a period) yields only partial topical matches; apply before answering to diversify queries and require direct evidence.
content: When a question asks about a specific past event (e.g., what someone shared, made, photographed, or posted in a given period) and no retrieved memory explicitly asserts the full claim (subject + object + time), do not answer from the closest topical matches.

Run at least one additional search before answering, varying the content terms: combine the subject and time window with synonyms/terms from the event's activity and likely outcome domain instead of repeating the topic that dominated the first results.
For such event questions, memories about plans, habits, preferences, or recurring topics are circumstantial; answer only when a retrieved memory directly asserts the event's object.

payload.name: ComplementQueryForBesidesQuestions
payload.description: When the user asks for activities, hobbies, or interests besides/apart from an explicitly named topic, use structured and expanded searches that do not let that topic dominate.
content: When the question asks for activities, hobbies, or interests 'besides', 'apart from', or 'other than' an explicitly named topic (e.g., yoga), do not build the main query around that topic, or results will be dominated by memories about it.

Construct the query around the general category (e.g., 'activities', 'hobbies', 'interests', 'pursuits') while omitting the excluded topic, and include concrete alternative terms from the person's known context.

Use structured search with relevant predicates (e.g., predicate='activity') to retrieve diverse activity memories, and increase top_k or issue multiple searches with varied expansions so less central activities are not crowded out.

After retrieval, discard memories whose content is primarily about the excluded topic, check whether the retrieved set covers distinct concrete activities, and if not, search again with additional expansions.

payload.name: Broaden Recommendation Retrieval Beyond Recipient and Date
payload.description: Use when a question asks what one person recommended to another and direct search with both names and date returns no match.
content: If initial search for a recommendation from A to B on a date returns no memory naming both A and B or the date, run an additional hybrid search using only A plus the item category with time_mode none, and inspect current versions of top results.
Treat statements that A read, watched, finished, or highly recommends an item as supporting a recommendation even if B and the exact date are absent; do not require all question entities to match.

payload.name: Exhaustive retrieval for category enumeration questions
payload.description: When a user asks for a list of items in a category (hobbies, interests, activities, possessions, preferences, etc.), use this skill before answering.
content: Before answering an enumeration-of-category question, run multiple searches with distinct query formulations and keywords targeting the category and its possible sub-items; do not stop after the first hybrid search.

Inspect results from all memory kinds (preference, event, plan, profile) and include any memory that mentions the subject's engagement, interest, or intention regarding the category, even if the memory's main topic is different.
Continue searching until an additional search returns no new distinct candidate members, then aggregate the full set into the answer and cite all supporting evidence.

payload.name: Category-Instance Search Diversification
payload.description: Use when a question asks to enumerate instances of a category (activities, hobbies, interests, foods) and initial retrieval yields no clear instance.
content: When a question asks to enumerate instances of a category (activities, hobbies, interests, foods, etc.), derive candidate instance terms from the question, from any retrieved memories, and from common subcategories; run separate searches for each candidate term combined with the subject.

If a search for category instances returns only peripherally related memories (e.g., a company, a place) and no concrete instance, reformulate the query with synonyms and specific examples of the category before concluding; do not rerun the same query with only depth or top_k changed.

payload.name: Find competing interests for delayed activity
payload.description: Use when asked why a person sometimes delays, skips, or puts off a regular activity.
content: Before answering why someone sometimes delays or omits a recurring activity, run an additional semantic or keyword search for that person's other hobbies, interests, and preferred activities (e.g., query '<person> hobbies and interests').

If the retrieved memories only describe the activity itself or direct mentions of delay, treat evidence as insufficient and expand the search to competing interests; a strong competing interest can explain the delay even if it never mentions the delayed activity.

payload.name: Corroborate List-Answer Items with Targeted Searches
payload.description: Use when a question asks for the ways, methods, or items a person uses for an activity and a retrieved memory mentions a candidate item.
content: Gather candidate items from both event memories and preference memories (e.g., what the person prefers, likes, or uses).
If a candidate item is supported by only one retrieved memory, run a targeted search using the item term combined with the person's name to find corroborating or contradicting memories.
Include preference-oriented query variants such as 'prefers', 'likes', 'uses', 'enjoys' alongside action-oriented terms like 'methods', 'ways', 'enhances' when retrieving evidence.

payload.name: Count-event-mentions-with-inflections
payload.description: Use when a question asks how many times someone performed an activity (won, played, mentioned, etc.).
content: For counting questions about past actions, first list morphological variants of the action verb (e.g., win/wins/won/winning) and both singular/plural object nouns (game/games).
Issue keyword searches for each variant and combine with semantic/hybrid search to retrieve memories phrased differently; do not assume a single query captures all mentions.

payload.name: Count Owned Items via Acquisition Events
payload.description: Use when a question asks how many of an item a person has or owns as of a time.
content: When asked for a count of items a person owns/has, search for concrete acquisition or ownership events: adopted, bought, received, owns, has a [item], or named instances of the item.
Do not make 'number', 'count', or 'how many' the primary query terms; these often miss individual event memories.
Enumerate distinct named entities/instances from retrieved memories and sum them only when each event clearly indicates a separate item owned by the person.
If retrieval returns only plans, considerations, or other people's items, continue searching with alternative terms before answering 'no information'.

payload.name: Retrieve Generic Creative Work Descriptions
payload.description: When a question asks what a specific creative work (screenplay, book, film, project) is about, use before hybrid search to also query generic descriptors like 'creative project' and 'completed project' and inspect event/achievement memories.
content: When the user asks about the subject of a specific creative work, do not restrict search to the exact artifact term and ordinal; include query expansions and keywords using generic descriptors such as 'creative project', 'completed project', 'recent work', plus thematic/content words from the question.

If initial results contain no memory stating the completed work's subject, search or inspect event memories with predicates like achievement or completion rather than only in-progress plans or titles, since completed works may be stored generically.

Judge evidence sufficiency against all retrieved current related memories, not only those mentioning the exact artifact type; a memory describing a completed creative project with matching themes can satisfy the question.

payload.name: Include event memories for current-activity queries
payload.description: When a query asks what someone is currently reading, doing, working on, or otherwise engaged in, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'state'; search both 'state' and 'event' memories because ongoing activities are often stored as events.
content: If a question asks about a person's current activity (e.g., currently reading, working on, building, studying), set memory_kinds to include both 'state' and 'event', or omit the memory_kinds filter, since ongoing activities are typically stored as event memories.
If a search restricted to 'state' returns no supporting evidence for an activity question, retry with broader memory_kinds before answering 'no information available'.

payload.name: Date-specific discussion topic recovery
payload.description: When a question asks what named people discussed or the topic of a conversation on a specific date, use this to require date-aligned evidence and per-participant event searches.
content: When answering what X and Y discussed on a specific date, search each participant's individual events for that date; discussion topics are often stored as separate personal events, not as a joint 'discussion' memory.
Verify that every evidence memory's time range covers the target date; if no date-matching evidence is retrieved, run additional searches with participant names and the date before answering.
Treat 'topic' as possibly multiple topics; combine all date-matching memories rather than stopping at the first candidate.

payload.name: Date-bounded event retrieval with count verification
payload.description: When a question asks for events within a specific date range or month, use explicit temporal filters and verify all expected events are retrieved before answering, including follow-up synonym searches when the count seems incomplete.
content: If the question specifies a date range or month, use structured or hybrid search with world_start/world_end filters covering that whole range instead of relying only on natural-language temporal phrases in the query.

Before answering a count question, verify the retrieved evidence satisfies the requested count; if not, issue additional searches using synonyms for likely milestone event types such as marriage, birth, pregnancy, move, or job change.
Do not treat a later announcement or related mention as evidence that the underlying event occurred in the target period; check the event's world_start date.

payload.name: Date-specific retrieval follow-up
payload.description: When a query asks about an event on a specific date and the first memory search returns no event on that date, run an additional search using the date and subject before answering no information.
content: If a user question contains a concrete date and a subject (person/entity), and your initial retrieval returned no memory whose world_start matches that date, perform at least one additional search that combines the subject with the date as a keyword or structured filter before answering 'no information'.
Do not rely only on semantic similarity for date-specific questions; use date-filtered or keyword retrieval to catch events whose phrasing differs from the query.

payload.name: Decompose Multi-Condition Retrieval Queries
payload.description: Use when a question requires intersecting two independent facts about a subject.
content: When a question requires intersecting two independent facts about a subject (e.g., an activity they enjoy AND a pet they own), run separate retrieval passes: one per condition. Do not rely on a single combined query.
Vary query terms per pass: for enjoyment/hobbies use terms like enjoys, getting into, trying, hobby, activity; for possession/relationship use terms like adopted, has, owns, pet, dog.
Answer only when evidence covers both conditions. If one side is missing, issue additional targeted searches for that condition before finalizing.

payload.name: Direction-Sensitive Recommendation Recall
payload.description: Use when a question asks what recommendations, advice, suggestions, or pointers one person received from another.
content: Fix the direction: the source is the person who gave; the recipient is the person who received. Build query expansions such as '<source> recommended/advised/suggested to <recipient>' and '<recipient> was recommended/advised by <source>'.
Filter retrieved memories by direction: exclude memories where the recipient recommended, supported, or gave advice to the source.

When the top results are all reverse-direction or supportive-only, run extra searches for '<source> advice to <recipient>' and '<source> inspired <recipient>' and include memories where the recipient's plan or action is explicitly attributed to the source's advice or setup.
Answer only from memories whose evidence assigns the source as the giver and the recipient as the receiver; if none are found, do not substitute reverse-direction memories as evidence.

payload.name: Expand emotion-word queries to behavioral evidence
payload.description: Use when a question asks about a frustration, problem, difficulty, or recurring issue.
content: When the question uses an emotional label such as 'frustration', 'problem', or 'difficulty', do not search only those literal words; add expansions that capture the underlying situation: 'searching for', 'looking for', 'has not found', 'unable to find', 'struggling with', 'wants to find'.
For recurring frustrations or repeated issues, combine concrete behavior/object terms with frequency terms such as 'every week', 'weekly', 'always', 'keeps', or 'ritual'.
Prefer explicit recurrence statements as evidence over indirect, one-time, or jocular mentions.
If the first search returns no direct match, issue at least one alternate retrieval using the concrete activity before concluding the information is unavailable.

payload.name: Emotion-location answers need activity-place searches
payload.description: Use when a question asks which places give a person peace, calm, joy, or similar positive emotion.
content: If the question asks for places/locations that give a person a positive emotion (peace, calm, joy, comfort), run at least two searches: one with the emotion-focused phrasing and one that combines the person's known activities (e.g., yoga, meditation, walking) with candidate place types (beach, park, trail, home, retreat, garden).
Before listing a place in the answer, require a retrieved memory that connects that place to the person AND contains an emotion/calm descriptor, preferring the most recent version of the memory.
When the first search returns only generic places, broaden with location nouns and activity nouns in the query instead of simply increasing top-k or using the same query again.

payload.name: Infer enjoyment from genre preferences
payload.description: Use when a question asks whether someone would enjoy a named author or creative work, and memory may contain that person's genre or style preferences.
content: When a question asks whether a person would enjoy a specific author, book, movie, or other creative work, first retrieve and review the person's genre and style preferences from memory.

If the person's preferred genres are visible in memory, identify the genre of the named author/work and match it against those preferences; explicit memories about that exact author or work are not required for a judgment.

Do not answer 'No information available' when preference evidence exists and the author/work's genre can be reasonably identified; reserve that answer for cases where no preference evidence was found.

payload.name: Entity-name questions: retry with attribute-free query
payload.description: When a question asks to identify an entity by descriptive attributes and a date, and the direct search with those attributes fails to return a memory naming the entity, retry a minimal query before answering.
content: When the question asks to name an entity (e.g., a game, movie, book) from descriptive attributes and a date, and the initial hybrid or keyword search does not return any memory containing a plausible entity of that type, retry with a minimal query containing only the subject, the entity type, and the date/date range (e.g., 'game' + date), omitting the descriptive adjectives that may not appear verbatim in stored memories.

If the fallback returns a memory that mentions several activities or titles for that period, inspect it and select the entity whose type matches the question, even if the memory describes the activity as 'mentioned', 'enjoyed', or 'watched' rather than with the question's exact wording.

payload.name: Enumeration via Category Vocabulary Search
payload.description: Use when a question asks to list or enumerate items a person made, bought, or created for a category.
content: Before answering an enumeration question about items bought/created for a beneficiary class (e.g., pets, children, household), identify the class and generate a broad list of concrete category items (for pets: beds, collars, tags, toys, leashes, food, grooming supplies; for children: clothes, toys, books, furniture).
Run at least one additional keyword or hybrid search using these category terms even if prior searches returned memories, and inspect any newly retrieved candidates before finalizing the answer.
When a memory mentions a specific completed or ongoing artifact of a category, treat it as evidence for that category even if the memory's main topic is another event or experience.

payload.name: Enumeration-Question Synonym-Expanded Searches
payload.description: Use when a question asks how a person did something and expects a list of actions.
content: When a question asks 'How did <entity> <outcome>?' or 'What actions did <entity> take?', treat it as an enumeration request whose answer may span multiple distinct activities stored in separate memories.

Before answering, if the initial retrieval returns only some action memories, run additional searches using action-oriented synonyms and paraphrases of the target verb/outcome (e.g., for 'promote': marketing, advertising, partner, collaboration, launch, campaign, showcase, content, video) to surface memories that describe the same activity category with different wording.

Check sufficiency after each search: if the question asks for 'how' and new searches keep finding different actions, continue until no new distinct actions appear; do not finalize an answer after a single top-k retrieval when the question is enumerative.

payload.name: Retrieve event date for temporal-context questions
payload.description: When a question asks which holiday, holiday season, or time of year coincides with a specific event, retrieve the event and its date first, then infer the season from the date; do not stop after one search that misses the event.
content: When a question asks which holiday, holiday season, or time of year coincides with an event (e.g., wedding, birthday, trip), first retrieve the event memory and its world_start date. Use event synonyms (got married/wedding, was born/birthday) and do not require the holiday or season name to appear in the query or memory text.

If the event memory provides a date but no holiday name, determine the holiday or season from the calendar date (e.g., late December → Christmas season) using general world knowledge, and answer from that date as evidence.

Do not conclude 'No information available' after a single retrieval when the question asks about an event's temporal context; run at least one additional search focused on the event and its date before answering.

payload.name: Exhaustive Retrieval for List and Count Questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks for a list or count of entities or events and initial retrieval may be incomplete.
content: When the question asks for a list or count of entities/events, treat it as an exhaustive retrieval: do not stop after the first top-k search.
Issue additional searches using synonyms and related terms (e.g., 'won', 'participated', 'tournament', 'competition') and increase top-k/depth until the last search returns no new relevant memories.

Before answering, aggregate every distinct event memory that matches the counted activity; verify that the answer equals the total number of distinct events found, not just the first retrieved subset.

Do not treat a single failed keyword search as proof that an event never occurred; expand the query to the subject's associated activities and roles, then re-judge evidence sufficiency before concluding absence.

payload.name: Verify explicit event timing evidence
payload.description: When a question asks when an event happened (finished, completed, started), require evidence that explicitly states that event's timing; do not substitute a related event's date (publication, exhibit, announcement).
content: When a question asks when an event happened (finished, completed, started, created), verify the cited memory explicitly describes that event and its timing. Do not answer with the date of a related event (publication, exhibition, announcement) unless a memory explicitly equates that date with the requested event's time.

If retrieved memories only concern related events or lack explicit timing for the requested event, judge the evidence insufficient and run additional searches using temporal/completion phrases (e.g., 'completed', 'finished', 'a few days ago', 'recently') and structured filters on the relevant subject/predicate (e.g., artwork/created/completed).

When a search returns a memory with explicit relative timing (e.g., 'a few days ago'), resolve the date from the memory/session timestamp and cite that memory as evidence rather than the related-event memory.

payload.name: Search plan memories for future attendance questions
payload.description: When a user asks when someone is attending, going to, or planning a future event, include plan memories in retrieval and expand around intention verbs.
content: When a question asks about a future or scheduled activity (e.g., 'when is X attending...', 'when will X go to...'), run retrieval with memory_kind including both 'plan' and 'event' since future intentions may be stored as plan memories with world_start dates.
If the initial results contain no direct date, re-query with expansions such as 'plans to attend', 'will attend', 'scheduled to attend', 'next month/week' and do not restrict to event kind.
Use the world_start of a retrieved plan memory as the temporal anchor for answering 'when' questions.

payload.name: Search plan and event kinds for future-plan questions
payload.description: When answering questions about future events, planned activities, or what someone is planning for an upcoming time, include plan memories in retrieval; do not restrict memory_kinds to event only.
content: If the question asks about a future event, plan, or upcoming activity, search with memory_kinds covering both 'plan' and 'event' (for example ["plan", "event"]).
Do not filter memory_kinds to only 'event' for forward-looking questions; planned future events are often stored as 'plan' memories.
Before answering, check whether an additional retrieval over 'plan' memories could supply direct evidence, especially when initial results contain only related context.

payload.name: Implicit-Suggestion Recall via Agreement and Plan Memories
payload.description: Use when a question asks what suggestions, recommendations, or advice one person gave another and initial retrieval returns only general support or encouragement.
content: Run additional searches from the recipient's perspective: '<recipient> agreed to try', '<recipient> plans to switch to', '<recipient> is trying', combined with the question's topic keywords.

Also issue a structured search for plan or event memories whose subject is the recipient and whose predicate/object indicates a commitment or change, because such memories often imply the giver's suggestion.

Before answering, check that the retrieved evidence actually enumerates the requested items; if it does not, do not answer from general support memories—either search again for the specific items or state the unsupported portion explicitly.

payload.name: Include preference memories when enumerating consumed or favorite items
payload.description: When a question asks what a person has read, watched, liked, or consumed, do not restrict the search to event memories; include preference memories too.
content: If the question asks for a list or factual enumeration of a person's read/watched/liked/consumed items (e.g., books, movies, shows, foods, hobbies), run the initial search without a restrictive memory_kind filter, or explicitly include both 'event' and 'preference' memory kinds.

When the first search only returns vague descriptions or fails to name concrete items, repeat the search with preference memories included and inspect any preference memories returned, since they often hold specific titles and ongoing favorites.

payload.name: Instance-list retrieval for category questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks for specific examples/instances of a category (games, movies, books, foods, hobbies) for a subject, and the first generic search returns only broad statements without named items.
content: If a question asks for a list of specific items of a category (e.g., games, movies, books, hobbies) associated with a subject, and an initial generic-category search returns only broad descriptions without naming any items, do not end the search yet.

Run additional targeted searches combining the subject's name with category-related activity terms (e.g., 'plays', 'watched', 'recommends', 'enjoys', 'won'), and also search for the category itself in conjunction with related contexts (e.g., 'tournament', 'recommendation'). Inspect event, achievement, and preference memories because they often contain the specific named items.
Only produce 'No information available' after multiple varied searches fail to surface any specific named instances.

payload.name: Search beyond excluded activity for alternatives
payload.description: When a question asks what activity a person or group planned/did instead of a known activity, use this to avoid over-anchoring retrieval on the excluded activity.
content: If the user asks for an alternative, replacement, or activity done instead of a previously mentioned activity, do not build all searches and keywords around the excluded activity; the supporting memory may omit that activity entirely.

Run additional searches using the subject person/group plus substitution intent terms such as 'instead', 'alternative', 'planned to', and 'decided to', and search broadly for shared plans, preferences, or recent events involving the same people.

Before answering, inspect retrieved memories that mention plans or shared activities for those people even if they do not mention the excluded activity; select the memory that explicitly states the alternative plan rather than the first semantically similar result.

payload.name: PersonalAttributeLifeStageInference
payload.description: When asked about a person's age or other personal attribute and direct memory lacks the answer, use life-stage cues in retrieved or additional searches (education, work, relationship) to give a bounded uncertain inference instead of replying 'no information'.
content: When a user asks for a personal attribute (age, occupation, marital status) and no memory directly states it, run additional searches using related life-stage terms (e.g., for age: school, study, classes, finals, internship, graduate; for occupation: work, job, career; for marital status: partner, married, spouse).

Treat life-stage cues found in retrieved memories (e.g., attending classes, studying for finals, interning) as evidence for a bounded inference about the attribute, and express the uncertainty explicitly (e.g., 'likely in her 20s or early 30s, since she is in school').
Only answer 'no information available' after both direct and indirect life-stage searches fail to surface any relevant evidence.

payload.name: Location Retrieval from Implicit and Sub-Region Evidence
payload.description: Use when a question asks about a person's location, visited places, or country/state, and direct evidence may be missing or use different vocabulary.
content: When answering location questions, do not rely only on explicit travel or location terms. Run additional searches using the person's name with location-related keywords, event/plan terms, and sub-region names (cities, landmarks) to find memories that imply presence.
Treat memories of activities at named places (e.g., photo, conversation, game) as evidence of being in that place, and infer the containing country/state from city or landmark mentions.
Before concluding no information, perform time-filtered searches when a specific period is given, and use visit synonyms (visited, went to, has been to) in queries.
When counting visits, treat each distinct presence at a city or location within a country as a visit to that country, using timestamps to separate occurrences.

payload.name: Query Expansion and Completeness for Enumerative Questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks for a list or enumeration of items, members, or instances, or uses abstract or category terms that may not match memory wording.
content: When a question asks for a list or enumeration (e.g., which members, what items, which places, what experiences), treat it as a completeness query: after any hit, run additional searches pairing each known or role-based entity with concrete synonyms and hyponyms of the category.

If the question uses an abstract or superordinate term, expand the search with concrete specific terms likely to appear in memory (e.g., 'accident', 'injury', 'workshop', 'course', 'contest', 'diagnosed').
For multi-subject or multi-facet questions, run a separate targeted search for each named subject or facet, and use keyword/BM25 to catch long merged memories that may fall below semantic top-k.

Before finalizing an enumerative answer, verify that all plausible entities, facets, or instances have supporting evidence or an explicit search attempt; do not answer 'No information available' after a single unhelpful result set.
When the question demands a specific named entity, require verbatim evidence of that entity in retrieved memory content; otherwise continue searching rather than settling for a generic description.

payload.name: Non-primary goal search across memory kinds
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's goals, plans, or aspirations that are distinct from their primary skill/domain, include preference, event, and plan memory kinds and search concrete non-primary activity terms before answering.
content: When answering questions about a person's goals, aspirations, career plans, or intentions (especially goals distinct from their primary skill), do not restrict retrieval to only 'profile' and 'state' memory kinds. Include 'preference', 'event', and 'plan' kinds, because goals and off-the-field ambitions are commonly stored there.

When the question contrasts goals with the person's main domain, search with concrete terms for that person's non-primary activities (e.g., endorsements, charity, brand, business, community) in addition to negated goal phrases, and inspect memories that mention these activities even if initial scores are low.

payload.name: ExpandSearchForOngoingCreativeWork
payload.description: When a question asks what kind of fiction, stories, or creative work someone writes or creates, and the first search returns only interests, preferences, or older writings, run additional event-focused searches before answering.
content: Before answering what kind of stories or creative work someone produces, treat a single literal-query search as insufficient if it returns only preferences, interests, or older articles.
Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search for recent event memories using phrases such as 'currently working on', 'writing', 'struggling with', or 'challenge'.
If a recovered event memory explicitly describes the current work and a notable feature that directly answers the question, include that feature in the answer.

payload.name: OrdinalEventDateRetrieval
payload.description: When a question asks for the date of an ordinal occurrence (e.g., third win, first visit), search broadly for base-event memories and use world_start timestamps, including relative-time references, to infer the date.
content: When a question asks when an ordinal event (second, third, nth) happened, do not search only with the ordinal and explicit date words; issue additional searches using the base event without the ordinal (e.g., 'tournament win' if asked 'third tourney win').

Treat memory world_start as date evidence even if the text expresses time relatively ('last week', 'yesterday'); use the session or message timestamp to resolve the relative reference into a concrete date before deciding.

Before answering an ordinal-date question, collect all candidate event memories from multiple searches, sort them by world_start, and identify the requested ordinal by chronological order; do not assume the only explicitly dated memory is the requested ordinal.

payload.name: Origin-focused retrieval for introduction questions
payload.description: When a question asks how someone was introduced to, started, or first became involved in an activity, run an origin-focused search before answering.
content: If the user asks how a person was introduced to or started an activity/interest, do not answer from current-state memories about that activity alone.

Run an additional search with origin-oriented expansions (e.g., 'since childhood', 'first started', 'introduced by', 'early years') and inspect composite memories that mention family or early context even if their main topic is unrelated.

payload.name: Broaden memory kinds for ownership-duration questions
payload.description: When a question asks how long a person has had, owned, or possessed something, include profile and relationship memory kinds; do not restrict search to event memories only.
content: If the question asks how long someone has had/owned/possessed something (duration, since when, for how many years), run at least one search that includes memory_kinds profile and relationship in addition to event; ownership durations are often stored as profile facts.
If the first search returns only activity/event memories, broaden memory_kinds to include profile and relationship before concluding the fact is absent.

payload.name: Per-Entity Expansion for Intersection Queries
payload.description: Use when a question asks what two or more entities share or have in common.
content: If the initial search for a multi-entity intersection query returns no overlap, do not repeat the identical query; issue separate searches for each entity using its name and known aliases.

After each per-entity search, collect concrete attribute values (cities, activities, preferences) from retrieved memories and issue follow-up searches combining each entity with those candidate values.
Conclude 'no information' only after per-entity searches for all entities and candidate-value expansions have been attempted and still yield no supporting memory.

payload.name: Search general hobbies for activity-during-period questions
payload.description: When a question asks what activity a person does during a specific time or condition (e.g., while healing, during recovery, in their free time), before answering, also search for that person's general hobbies, interests, or pastimes without repeating the time/condition qualifier.
content: If a user asks what activity someone does during a stated period or condition (e.g., while healing, during vacation, on weekends), run a supplementary memory search with queries like '<person> hobbies', '<person> interests', and '<person> activities' without the period qualifier. Such preferences are often stored independently of the period.
When judging evidence sufficiency for these questions, do not require memories to mention the period; a hobby or pastime stated generally can be the correct activity during that period.

payload.name: Re-search post-event plans with domain terms
payload.description: When a question asks about a subject's plans after a specific event and the first search returns only the event memory, use domain/goal terms and time-bounded retrieval to locate the post-event plan memory.
content: When a question asks what plans or actions a subject has after a specific event (e.g., after advice, a meeting, a networking event), and the first search returns the event memory but no resulting plans, run an additional search using domain/goal terms inferred from the event context and the subject's goals, and restrict the time window to memories with world_start on or after the event date.
Do not answer with older, unrelated plan memories; if the re-search still yields no post-event plan memory, inspect the subject's memories dated from the event onward before finalizing an answer.

payload.name: Retrieve preference memories for ideal/preference questions
payload.description: When a question asks what someone thinks an ideal or preferred version of something should be, search for preference-kind memories and use attribute-level query terms before answering.
content: When the question asks for a person's ideal, preferred, or favorite version of an entity (e.g., ideal studio, dream home, favorite recipe), run a structured memory search with memory_kind='preference' in addition to the general hybrid search.

Use attribute-level query terms in expansions that target concrete features of the entity (e.g., flooring, location, lighting, layout, materials) because preference memories often describe specific attributes rather than the general topic.

If the initial top-k results contain only event/state memories about the entity and the question targets desired attributes, run at least one additional search with a higher top-k or a preference-focused query before answering.

payload.name: Expand Recommendation Queries to Preference Memories
payload.description: Use when a question asks what one person recommends or suggests for another and initial search yields no direct evidence.
content: Before answering a recommendation question, issue at least one search combining the recommender's name with preference vocabulary: 'enjoys', 'likes', 'plays', 'reads', 'watches', 'favorite', 'interested in', or 'hobby'.
If no retrieved memory explicitly links the recommender to the recommendation, search again using preference phrasing before concluding evidence is insufficient.

When a memory records the recommender's own preferred items in the question's category, treat it as candidate evidence for what they would recommend; verify the category matches and answer from that evidence.

payload.name: Require Explicit Preference Evidence and Multi-Query Retrieval
payload.description: Use when a question asks for a list of things a person likes/enjoys and the first search yields few or generic results.
content: Do not rely on a single incidental event or plan; search for explicit preference statements using terms like 'favorite', 'loves', 'enjoys', 'prefers' combined with category words.

If the first retrieval returns off-topic or only weakly related memories, run follow-up searches for each plausible subcategory, and filter by memory_kind 'preference' when available, until you find multiple explicit mentions or exhaust distinct formulations.
Cite only memories that state or clearly imply the person likes the item; an event alone is insufficient evidence of a general preference unless corroborated.

For favorite/preference questions, also run an additional search over event memories using positive-evaluation terms (e.g., 'found delicious', 'loved', 'enjoyed') together with the item or category, and treat such events as supporting evidence.

payload.name: Include preference memories for hobby questions
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's hobby, interest, or long-term activity (e.g., 'started practicing a few years ago', 'enjoys doing'), apply this before searching memory.
content: When the question targets a hobby, interest, or long-term activity, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; include 'preference' (and other relevant kinds) because such facts are often stored as preference records.

If the first event-only search does not surface a memory that explicitly names the hobby and its duration, retry with memory_kinds including 'preference' (and 'profile'/'state' as appropriate), and avoid a time range that excludes older preference records.
Treat a preference memory that states the hobby and how long the person has enjoyed it as sufficient evidence; do not require a matching event entry.

payload.name: Retrieve Preference Memories for Subjective Questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks what a person misses, likes, loves, values, or wants and initial hybrid results only restate behavior.
content: Run at least one structured memory search filtered to memory_kind=preference for that person, in addition to the hybrid search.

If initial results contain only indirect event/state restatements, issue another search with the person's name and terms like 'misses', 'loves', 'finds soothing', 'prefers', using a higher top_k and inspecting the newest version of each returned memory ID.
Prefer the content of the newest enriched version of a relevant memory over older versions or indirect paraphrases; answer only from visible evidence.

payload.name: Search projects across plan and event memory kinds
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's projects, plans, or future intentions, do not restrict search to plan memories alone; include event and other memory kinds that may describe projects or interests.
content: When the question asks about someone's projects, plans, or what they want to do, search across both 'plan' and 'event' memory kinds; projects and intentions are often stored as events with predicate 'project'.

If a first search with memory_kinds=['plan'] returns only tangential results, rerun with a broader kind set (e.g., plan, event, state) and include keywords from the question's subject and domain before answering.

payload.name: Psychological-state synonym search
payload.description: Use when a question asks how someone stays or becomes confident, motivated, positive, or keeps going.
content: If the user asks how a person maintains or achieves a psychological state (e.g., confidence, motivation, positivity), run at least one extra search using synonyms of that state (motivated, encouraged, determined, positive, strong) combined with strategy phrases like 'strategies for staying', 'ways to keep', 'support system', 'goals', 'reasons for starting'.

Treat memories that describe the person's motivation, encouragement, or coping strategies as relevant evidence for confidence-related questions, and do not depend on the exact keyword from the question appearing in the memory.

During questions about a person's inspiration or motivation, treat 'validation', 'achievement', 'recognition', and 'positive feedback' as potential inspiration sources; run additional hybrid searches for these terms before concluding.

After each retrieval round, verify whether the evidence covers all plausible answer components; if a component remains unsupported, issue another search with broader semantic expansions instead of answering immediately.

payload.name: DualSearchForRecommendations
payload.description: When a question asks for a hobby, activity, or recommendation related to a person's stated interest, use this Skill to search for existing hobbies/skills in addition to the interest and consider combinations.
content: When a question asks for a recommendation related to a stated interest, run at least two semantic searches: one for the stated interest with recommendation keywords, and one for the person's existing skills, activities, and hobbies without referencing the interest.

If the first search returns only surface matches (e.g., travel clubs) and no clear integrated candidate, expand queries to combine the found skills with the interest (e.g., 'writing about travel', 'travel blogging') before answering.
Before answering, verify that retrieved evidence contains both the stated interest and a relevant existing activity; if not, issue additional searches rather than answering from partial evidence.

payload.name: Relational-role to meeting-event retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks when a subject first met a person identified only by a relational role (future wife, fiancée, partner, spouse) and direct role-based hits are missing, apply this retrieval pattern.
content: Before answering 'no information,' when the question uses a relational role label for a person, expand searches to include meeting/encounter verbs (met, met up, went on a trip/date with) and descriptive terms from other memories that could identify that person (nationality, names, attributes).

If a later relationship memory is found (marriage, engagement, pregnancy, partner status), use it to identify the person, then search for the earliest meeting or trip event before that memory's date and report that event's time as the meeting.
Only a memory that explicitly describes the meeting or first encounter can establish the meeting time; do not infer it from the later relationship event alone.

payload.name: Relative-time expansion and evidence time check for temporal questions
payload.description: When a question specifies a time period and memories may store relative dates, expand searches with relative-time variants based on the session timestamp and answer only from memories whose time window overlaps asked period.
content: When a question specifies a time period (e.g., 'second week of November', 'last month'), expand search queries with the relative-time expressions equivalent to that period as measured from the session timestamp (e.g., 'last Friday', 'last week', 'this month'), because memories often store relative dates.

After retrieval, before answering a temporal question, verify each candidate memory's world_start/world_end overlaps the asked time period; discard any candidate whose time window is outside the period even if its semantic or keyword score is high, and continue searching with time-focused variants.

Do not treat memories about future interest, plans, or preferences (e.g., 'expresses interest in visiting X', 'plans to visit X') as evidence of an actual past visit; require a memory that records the event itself within the asked time window.

payload.name: Temporal-anchor post-milestone retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks what someone did or planned after a dated milestone event (e.g., after a wedding) and the first search results appear unrelated or pre-date the event.
content: When a question asks what someone did or plans to do after a dated milestone event, use the milestone date as a temporal anchor; run searches with typical follow-up activity terms (honeymoon, celebration, get-together, trip, activity) and filter or rank memories with world_start on or after that date.
If the first retrieval returns only memories dated before the milestone, do not answer from them; re-search with additional related terms and compare time windows.
Treat pre-milestone memories as non-evidence for post-milestone questions even when they share location or activity vocabulary.

payload.name: Expand retrieval for shared personal achievements
payload.description: When a question asks what achievement or news one person shared with another, retrieve events about either person alone and use a broader time window instead of requiring both names and exact date.
content: If a query describes an item 'shared with' or 'told to' another person, search for memories whose subject is either person individually; the sharing may be implicit and the memory may mention only the achiever.
Use a broadened time window (e.g., whole stated month or relative phrases like 'last week') rather than a single point date, so recent personal milestones are not excluded.

payload.name: Shared-Activity Retrieval for Multi-Person Gift Questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks for a gift, plan, or recommendation suitable for two or more named people.
content: Run a retrieval that combines their names with concrete shared-activity terms (cooking, recipes, classes, hobbies, outings) in addition to abstract topic keywords.

Before answering, check that the proposed gift is supported by evidence for each intended recipient; if evidence supports only one person, search for a shared activity or interest instead of defaulting to one person's individual preference.

payload.name: Per-person profile search for shared-interest questions
payload.description: When a question asks what interests, hobbies, or preferences two or more people share, search each person's profile/hobby memories separately before answering.
content: When the question asks what two or more named people share (interests, hobbies, preferences, or similar traits), run a separate profile/hobby search for each person (e.g., query with the person's name and 'hobbies' or 'interests') in addition to a joint-activity search.

Do not treat plans to do something together, one-time joint events, or supportive gestures as evidence of a shared interest; require either an explicit shared-interest memory or overlapping individual profile/preference memories.
After initial retrieval, judge evidence sufficiency for the comparison: if the evidence only describes activities done or planned together, run the per-person profile searches again before answering.

payload.name: Short Phrase Search with Base Noun
payload.description: Use when a question asks for a short named attribute like a motto, slogan, nickname, or title and exact phrase search may miss inflected forms.
content: If the query asks about a short named attribute (motto, slogan, nickname, title), add the bare noun (e.g., 'motto') as a keyword in addition to any full phrase like 'family motto'.

When the first keyword search does not return a memory containing that attribute word, re-run with the base word alone and also perform a semantic or hybrid search before concluding no information is available.

payload.name: Structured-Search Speaker Statements
payload.description: Use when a question asks what a specific person said, recommended, or described about a specific place or topic.
content: Run a structured search with subject set to that person's name and a query containing the place/topic and its common synonyms or abbreviations.
Include at least one query expansion using likely descriptive language from stored memories (e.g., adjectives like 'amazing', nouns like 'culture', 'food') in addition to rephrasing the question.
If the first search yields no directly relevant result, retry with increased top_k (10-15) or a keyword-only search before answering 'No information available'.

payload.name: Subject-centric retry for theme queries
payload.description: Use when a question asks about a theme/pattern emerging in one person's life (especially 'as mentioned by another').
content: When a question asks about a theme, pattern, or trend emerging in a specific person's life, do not rely only on queries containing the abstract theme word or a mentioner's name; those terms may be absent from stored episodic memories.

If the first hybrid search returns only unrelated general memories, run at least one follow-up search focused on the subject's own recent activities, interactions, and encounters (e.g., subject + 'helping', 'encounters', 'recurring'), and do not include the abstract theme word or the other person's name.

Before answering, verify the retrieved evidence actually reflects the asked theme; if the evidence contains only generic plans, relationships, or unrelated events, continue searching the subject's discrete episodes until a recurring behavioral pattern is found or exhausted.

payload.name: Supplement Searches for Item Lists Across Related Contexts
payload.description: Use when a question asks for all items a person uses or prefers during an activity.
content: Do not answer from one exact-match retrieval. Run at least one additional search using related context terms such as meditation, relaxation, calming, focus, or associated settings.

When returning an item list, include distinct named items found in preference and event memories even if the memory says recommended, suggested, or calming rather than directly used during the activity.
Before finalizing, check whether the combined results cover all plausible named items from the related contexts; if a related-context search is still missing, refine keywords and search again.

payload.name: Broaden temporal filters for time-qualified retrieval
payload.description: When a question includes a specific time or date and a point-in-time filtered search returns no direct evidence, retry with a broader time range or no time filter before concluding the information is missing.
content: When a user question contains a specific time qualifier (e.g., 'in August 2022'), do not use a point-in-time filter as a hard constraint in the initial search; use a broader time range or omit the time filter, then assess temporal relevance from memory content and timestamps.
If a point-filtered search yields no directly supporting memory, retry the same query with a wider temporal window (or no time constraint) before answering that the information is absent.
Before using a retrieved memory as evidence, check its world_start/world_end against the question window; reject memories outside the window even if they are semantically similar.

payload.name: Retrieve interests for which-activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks which activity or hobby gives a person a benefit (e.g., escape, relaxation, imagination), retrieve the person's known interests from profile or preference memories and use them as candidate search terms.
content: When a question asks which activity or hobby gives a person a benefit, do not limit retrieval to memories that explicitly contain the benefit words. Retrieve the person's known hobbies/interests from profile or preference memories and treat them as candidate activities.
Before answering, run an additional memory search for each known interest/hobby term, and consider those results even if the benefit words are absent from the returned memory text.
If several interest memories compete, compare them using direct preference statements, frequency, and recency before selecting the answer.

payload.name: Extract nickname and name-variant details
payload.description: When a message directly addresses a known person using a nickname, shortened form, or alternative name, create a separate durable memory for the nickname even if the message also contains another fact.
content: During extraction, if a message addresses a known person using a nickname or name variant, generate a separate candidate recording that nickname (e.g., as a profile of the addressee or a relationship between speaker and addressee), in addition to any other candidates from the same message. Do not let a more salient event or state fact suppress this identity fact.

payload.name: Extract Duration from Relationship Statements
payload.description: Use when extracting facts from statements that include a duration for a relationship, membership, or repeated activity.
content: Treat explicit time-span phrases (e.g., 'for X years', 'for X months') as factual details whenever they qualify a relationship, group membership, role, or repeated activity; produce a candidate that records both the relationship/activity and its duration.
Do not skip extraction solely because the statement appears inside a rhetorical question or a casual conversational follow-up; the factual content still belongs in long-term memory.

payload.name: Capture addressees and inform recipients in event memories
payload.description: Use during extraction when a user's message directly addresses a named person or describes telling/announcing an event to others; record the recipient relationship alongside the event.
content: When a message opens by directly addressing a named person (e.g., 'Hey [Name]!') and then shares a personal life event, extract a memory that the speaker told that named person about the event, in addition to any memory about the event itself.

When a message mentions informing or announcing something to a group (work friends, family, etc.), preserve the act of informing explicitly in the memory content; do not let the memory only describe the group's reaction or support.

payload.name: Extract enumerated entity traits
payload.description: Use during extraction when a user message describes multiple entities in a group and assigns each a distinct attribute or personality; extract a separate candidate for each entity.
content: During extraction, when a message enumerates a group of entities (e.g., pets, children, employees) and assigns each a distinct attribute or personality, create one memory candidate per entity, preserving the order or specifier (e.g., oldest, second, youngest) in the memory text.
For stable personal traits such as temperament or preferences, use the `profile` memory type, ensure compactness, and link to the source message.

payload.name: Extract implied death from euphemistic language
payload.description: When extracting or updating memories, if a message implies a person is deceased through phrases like 'will never be able to...' or 'I miss him/her here', record the person as deceased or likely deceased instead of softening to a vague ability-based state.
content: During extraction, when a message strongly implies a person is deceased through phrases like 'will never be able to...', 'I miss him/her here', 'passed away', or 'is no longer with us', record the person's death as a durable state (e.g., subject is deceased) or event, rather than a softened paraphrase such as 'no longer able to support'.
Only infer death from clear euphemistic/loss language; do not infer from mere absence, distance, or 'I miss you' to someone who could still be alive.

During CRUD, when editing or merging memories, preserve or add an explicit deceased/likely-deceased state when the source evidence supports it, and avoid replacing it with vague ability-based phrasing.

payload.name: Extract Current Activity from Pleasantry-Prefixed Statements
payload.description: Use when a message begins with thanks or greetings but then explicitly states what the speaker is currently doing, writing about, or working on.
content: During extraction, do not skip a message merely because it opens with thanks or a pleasantry.
If the remainder explicitly describes the user's current ongoing activity, interest, or work topic, generate a compact state memory capturing that activity.
Keep the memory general, source-linked, and free of conversational filler.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Advice and Suggestions
payload.description: Use when a message contains explicit advice, recommendation, or suggestion from one speaker to another, including tentative or motivational phrasing.
content: During extraction, treat explicit advice, recommendations, or suggestions from one speaker to another as durable memory candidates, even when phrased tentatively (e.g., 'maybe look into', 'you should', 'keep trying').
Record the advisor, recipient, and the advised action or topic; use an allowed memory kind such as event or plan.
Do not skip such statements because they are conversational, motivational, or not yet acted upon.

payload.name: Extract Affirmative Possession Claims
payload.description: Use when a speaker affirms having the same kind of object or gift as a previous speaker.
content: During extraction, when a speaker responds affirmatively to a question about possessing an item or receiving a gift, create a separate candidate for that speaker's possession/event.
Do not treat the affirmative reply as duplicate of the prior speaker's candidate; each speaker's fact is distinct.

payload.name: Aggregate Repeated Location Visits into Count Memory
payload.description: Use when a subject's visits/trips to the same location are mentioned across multiple messages.
content: When extracting candidates, if a message describes a visit to a location already mentioned as visited by the same subject, extract a candidate that records the total number of visits, not only a new separate event.

During CRUD, when a candidate or existing memory contains a visit to a location and another memory records a different visit to the same location by the same subject, update or merge into one event memory that explicitly states the combined visit count.

payload.name: Extract All Explicitly Stated Plan Elements
payload.description: Use when a plan or event is described across multiple messages.
content: Treat each explicitly stated element of a plan or event as an extractable fact, even if it appears in an earlier message than the message that most clearly names the plan.

When multiple messages jointly describe one plan, either include all explicitly mentioned elements in a single candidate's content or create one candidate per element; never let a later, more prominent mention cause earlier distinct details to be omitted.

payload.name: Resolve Anaphora Before Extraction
payload.description: Use when a user statement contains a pronoun or demonstrative (it, this, that, they) referring to a previously mentioned entity.
content: Before extracting a memory candidate, resolve every pronoun and demonstrative to its nearest plausible antecedent in the conversation context; do not default to the speaker or the nearest noun in the same message.
Ground each candidate in its own source message; do not substitute nouns from other messages that appear in similar statements.
If the referent is ambiguous or unverifiable, omit the claim or mark it for review rather than assigning a wrong subject or object.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Approach-to-Challenges Statements
payload.description: Use when a message explicitly states how the speaker or their group handles tough situations or challenges.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit statement describing how the speaker or their group responds to challenges (e.g., backing each other up, not quitting, improving), generate a candidate memory capturing that approach as a state or preference.
Do not require the statement to be the main topic; extract it even when embedded in a longer reply that also mentions past events.
Link the candidate to the speaker's profile or group relationship, and record the source message and timestamp for provenance.

payload.name: Preserve Third-Party Attribution
payload.description: Use when a message attributes an emphasis, teaching, rule, or belief to a class, instructor, group, or organization.
content: When a source message attributes an emphasis, teaching, rule, or belief to a class, instructor, group, or organization, keep that entity as the subject of the memory content.
During both extraction and CRUD, preserve the original attribution; if the memory only records the speaker's perspective, add the entity-level claim as a separate, clearly attributed fact.

payload.name: Preserve notable direct quotes as verbatim memories
payload.description: When a message contains a distinctive, pithy, or emotionally salient direct quotation that a future question could ask about, create a memory that preserves the exact wording.
content: During extraction, identify direct quotations that are distinctive or memorable (e.g., a toast, motto, promise, or exact phrasing about a key event).
For such quotes, create an event or statement memory capturing the verbatim wording, attributed to the speaker and linked to the message.
Do not replace abstract summaries; add the quote memory alongside them so both gist and exact wording are retained.
Skip routine, trivial, or highly verbose statements where the exact wording is unlikely to be queried.

payload.name: Capture Explicit Reasons for Actions
payload.description: During memory extraction, when a message states what inspired or motivated an action, include that reason in the event memory instead of only recording the action.
content: During extraction, if a user explicitly states why they did something (e.g., what inspired or motivated the action), record that reason as part of the event memory or as a linked memory; do not drop it in favor of the action alone.
If the message contains both the action and its stated cause, combine them in one compact event memory so the motivation remains evidence-bound and retrievable.

payload.name: Capture explicitly stated motivations
payload.description: When a message pairs an action or routine with an explicit stated reason, value, or motivation (e.g., 'because', 'important to me'), capture that motivation as a preference or state memory.
content: During extraction, when a speaker states an action and explicitly explains why (using phrases like 'because', 'so that', 'is important to me', 'to help me'), extract the stated reason as a preference or state memory, and keep the activity fact in the same candidate or a linked memory.
Do not let an activity-only candidate substitute for the explicit motivation; both the behavior and its stated rationale are durable facts for future why-questions.

payload.name: Extract Discovery Source as Separate Memory
payload.description: Use when a user states how they heard about or discovered an event, place, or opportunity.
content: When the user explicitly states how they learned about an event or opportunity, create a separate event memory capturing the discovery source, in addition to any memory of the event itself.
Set memory_kind to 'event', subject to the speaker, and world_start to the session timestamp; include the concrete source and place.
Keep discovery-source memories distinct from the main event memory; do not merge them.

payload.name: Distinct repeated events as new memories
payload.description: When a candidate describes an event that is a distinct new occurrence (e.g., 'again', 'another', 'second', 'third', or a different date) of an activity already in memory, ADD a new event memory instead of UPDATEing the older one.
content: During CRUD, before choosing UPDATE, check whether the candidate event is a separate occurrence (different date/time or an ordinal/again marker) of an existing event memory. If it is a new occurrence, ADD a new event memory; reserve UPDATE for revising or enriching the same single occurrence.

Do not overwrite an older event with a newer similar event merely because both concern the same subject or activity type; preserving the history of past occurrences is needed for future counts or timelines.
Update or enrich only when the candidate clearly refers to the same occurrence as the existing memory (same event, same time frame); otherwise default to ADD.

payload.name: Extract explicit comfort and affection statements
payload.description: When a user explicitly states that an activity, pet, or person helps them cope, comfort, or that they love/affectionately evaluate someone or something, extract that as a preference or relationship memory.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states that an activity, pet, item, or person helps the user cope, stay distracted, feel better, or is loved/affectionately evaluated, create a candidate memory for each mentioned helper or subject.
Record the helper/subject in a compact memory: use preference for activities/items, relationship for pets/people, and include the role (e.g., 'helps during tough times', 'loved') in the content.
Do not skip a message solely because its event details were already captured; the evaluative statement is a separate durable fact. Attach the source message as evidence.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Preference Statements
payload.description: Use when a speaker explicitly states a preference, favorite, or enjoyment using affective language, even if brief, embedded, or phrased as additive.
content: During extraction, treat explicit self-referential preference statements using affective language ('love', 'like', 'enjoy', 'favorite', 'prefer', 'really into') as preference memory candidates, even if brief, embedded in a longer reply, or phrased as additive ('also', 'besides', 'one of my favorites').
Extract each distinct item named as liked/loved, preserving the object and intensity; do not skip because the statement is casual, secondary, or surrounded by unrelated context.
Do not downgrade explicit preferences into neutral states or event/plan memories; keep them as durable preference memories linked to the speaker.
Do not apply to hypothetical, third-party, negated, or inferred preferences without explicit affective language.

payload.name: Extract Explicit User-Stated Views
payload.description: When a user explicitly states how they view or regard something (e.g., 'feel like', 'view as', 'is like'), capture that stated view as a memory.
content: During extraction, when the user explicitly states how they view or regard an object (phrases such as 'feel like', 'view as', 'treat as', 'is like'), create a candidate memory that records the stated view.
Use a 'relationship' memory when the view connects the user to an object (e.g., user views X as family); otherwise use 'preference' for attitudes toward the object.
Do not require action-oriented evidence; a clear statement of how a user regards someone or something is durable information that should be extracted independently.

payload.name: Extract all distinct facts from multi-fact messages
payload.description: Use when a single message states multiple distinct durable facts, claims, or preferences that must each be captured.
content: During candidate extraction, treat each distinct claim in a message as a separate durable fact (skills, preferences, events, relationships) and generate one candidate per claim; do not let a single summary drop any claim.
When a sentence contains multiple clauses with different predicates, create a separate candidate for each clause rather than only the clause that seems to fit an existing memory narrative.
Before finalizing a candidate list, check each message for background facts that future questions could compare across people; do not let a concrete action candidate absorb them.
During batched ADD/UPDATE/MERGE, do not let a new candidate overwrite or merge away an existing memory claim that is still true; preserve all distinct true claims from the source.

payload.name: Extract all explicitly stated events
payload.description: When a message states a concrete past event, completion, start, or possession transfer with a time reference, extract it as a separate event memory during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, create a separate event candidate for every clearly stated event or fact in the message, even when the message's main topic is about something else.
Resolve relative time expressions (e.g., 'last Friday', 'when I was 10') using the message timestamp or speaker's age to set world_start.
Do not let a dominant topic, emotional wording, or lack of detail cause you to drop secondary events.
Record the exact item, action, and stated reason when present; do not substitute inferred categories or omit stated causes.
Do not convert completed past actions into current ongoing states; store them as event memories.

payload.name: Extract bonding shared-activity memories
payload.description: When a message describes a shared activity with a named person and ties it to bonding or memories, extract a candidate even if described informally.
content: During extraction, treat statements where the speaker says they did/do an activity with another person and calls it a way to bond, make memories, or grow closer as high-value event/relationship candidates, even when the activity is named generically (e.g., 'play games', 'gaming').

When the context unambiguously implies a conventional activity ('gaming' → video games, 'cards' → card games), extract that specific activity; otherwise record the activity at the level of specificity actually stated.
Do not fabricate relationship details or durations beyond the message; link the memory to the named person and keep the bonding/memories purpose as part of the memory evidence.

payload.name: Extract General Peace-and-Comfort Statements
payload.description: When a user says something gives them peace, comfort, or helps them cope during difficult times, extract it as a memory candidate even if phrased generally.
